options.headline: WHAT IS ALREADY GOING RIGHT
options.text: Most AI headlines are about what could go wrong. The stories below are about what has already gone right, and each one comes with a number. In Singapore, AI caught seven times more missed specialist referrals. In north-west England, care homes saw about a third fewer falls. In Spain, fewer sepsis patients needed intensive care. At Geisinger, AI-guided screening outreach was tied to 43% lower two-year mortality. And primary teachers got 49 minutes of planning time back.

options.headline: MORE ROOM FOR THE HUMAN PART
options.text: Purpose lives in the work only people can do: teaching a child, comforting a resident, calling a patient who needs a test. In these five stories, AI takes on the background work, reading thousands of clinical notes, watching for a fall, drafting a lesson, so people can give their attention where it counts. Nurses still make the calls. Staff still reach the resident. Teachers still teach. AI just helps them get there sooner.

options.headline: WHO CATCHES WHAT WE MISS?
options.text: Every system has gaps: a referral that never gets sent, a resident who falls with no one nearby, a patient overdue for screening. In these stories, AI watches those gaps so people can act, with seven times more missed referrals caught in Singapore, about a third fewer care-home falls in England, and fewer sepsis patients in intensive care in Spain. Where in your own work would a second pair of eyes help most?

options.headline: FIVE GAPS, NARROWER
options.text: Five measured results: missed referrals caught in Singapore, fewer care-home falls in England, fewer sepsis patients in intensive care in Spain, lower mortality after AI-guided cancer screening outreach in Pennsylvania, and less time spent on lesson planning for teachers.

options.headline: CATCHING WHAT SLIPS THROUGH
options.text: The common thread here is the thing that slips through the cracks. A specialist referral written in a note but never sent. A fall in a care home. A patient overdue for colon cancer screening. An early sign of sepsis. In each case AI flagged it and people acted, and the results show up as fewer falls, fewer intensive care stays and lower mortality.

stories.institution: National University Polyclinics / National University Health System, MR-AI missed-referral safety system (Singapore)
stories.teaser: AI catches specialist referrals that slipped through the cracks
stories.headline: AI raised detection of missed specialist referrals sevenfold in Singapore
stories.why: Quasi-experimental study at seven primary care clinics in Singapore, npj Digital Medicine
stories.bullet: Sevenfold more missed referrals caught, as AI read 25,000 notes a week
texts:
When a doctor's notes say a patient needs a specialist but no referral is ordered, that patient can fall through the cracks. At seven National University Polyclinics in Singapore, an AI safety system scanned about 25,000 consultation notes a week for exactly that gap.

It raised weekly detection of missed referrals an estimated sevenfold. The study is in npj Digital Medicine.

#AIforGood

Missed referrals are a quiet patient-safety problem. Singapore's National University Polyclinics use MR-AI to flag consultation notes that mention a referral with no matching order.

Of 428 flags, clinicians confirmed 225 missed referrals, and patients reported 31 more. The system was 99.9% specific, with an estimated 41 hours of staff time saved.

#AIforGood

What happens to the referral a doctor meant to make but didn't? In seven Singapore polyclinics, an AI system looked for it, reading about 25,000 notes a week and flagging gaps for clinicians to check.

Detection of missed specialist referrals rose an estimated sevenfold, with 256 cases found.

#AIforGood
stories.og_title: Accuracy and impact of an AI safety system for missed specialist referrals in primary care

stories.institution: Hospital Son Llàtzer (Palma, Spain), BIAlert-Sepsis AI alert
stories.teaser: An AI sepsis alert in Mallorca meant fewer ICU stays and lower costs
stories.headline: AI sepsis alerts cut ICU admissions and costs at a Spanish hospital
stories.why: Before-and-after study of 8,039 sepsis patients, PLOS Global Public Health
stories.bullet: Fewer septic patients needed intensive care, 30.4% vs 34.4%, with AI alerts
texts:
At Hospital Son Llàtzer in Palma, Spain, an AI model called BIAlert-Sepsis has flagged patients at risk of sepsis since 2019. Researchers compared 8,039 septic patients before and after it went live.

ICU admissions fell from 34.4% to 30.4%, hospital stays got shorter, and the average cost per admission dropped from 26,517 to 24,630 euros.

#AIforGood

Sepsis moves fast, and catching it early can keep patients out of intensive care. A hospital in Mallorca replaced its rule-based sepsis alert with an AI model.

After the switch, fewer septic patients needed the ICU, those who did stayed there for less time, and the hospital estimates savings of about 1,800 euros per patient. The study is in PLOS Global Public Health.

#AIforGood

What changes when a hospital's sepsis alert gets smarter? At Hospital Son Llàtzer in Spain, an AI model took over from a rule-based system in 2019.

Among 8,039 patients with sepsis, ICU admissions fell from 34.4% to 30.4%, with shorter stays on the wards and in intensive care.

#AIforGood
stories.og_title: Prospective economic evaluation of a predictive artificial intelligence model for sepsis: Effects on hospital costs and return on investment

stories.institution: NHS Lancashire and South Cumbria ICB / Lancaster University evaluation of Nobi AI ceiling lamps
stories.teaser: AI ceiling lamps in care homes cut falls by about a third
stories.headline: AI ceiling lamps in about 80 care homes cut resident falls by about a third
stories.why: Two-year evaluation across about 80 care homes by NHS Lancashire and South Cumbria and Lancaster University
stories.bullet: 32% fewer falls, as AI ceiling lamps watched over care home residents
texts:
About 32% fewer falls, and 23% fewer ambulance call-outs.

Across Lancashire and South Cumbria, around 800 AI ceiling lamps were fitted in about 80 care homes. Lancaster University's evaluation found falls dropped from 1.85 to about 1.28 per resident per month, and staff reached a fallen resident in under 3 minutes, down from 11.

#AIforGood

For an older person, a fall at night can mean a long wait on the floor before anyone comes.

In care homes across Lancashire and South Cumbria, AI ceiling lamps now alert staff the moment someone falls. Response times dropped from 11 minutes to under 3, and the playback helps staff spot what caused a fall and prevent the next one.

#AIforGood

Can a ceiling light keep someone safe?

In about 80 care homes in the north of England, AI lamps watch for falls and alert staff right away. An independent Lancaster University evaluation found about 32% fewer falls, and ambulance call-outs ending in a hospital trip fell by 24%.

#AIforGood
stories.source_name: NHS Lancashire and South Cumbria ICB, May 13, 2026

stories.institution: Oak National Academy Aila, evaluated by NFER for the Education Endowment Foundation
stories.teaser: An AI lesson assistant saved teachers 49 minutes a week
stories.headline: AI lesson assistant saved primary teachers 49 minutes a week, with no drop in quality
stories.why: Randomized trial of 464 teachers in 108 schools, independent NFER evaluation for the EEF
stories.bullet: 49 minutes a week saved, for teachers planning lessons with an AI assistant
texts:
49 minutes a week back for teachers.

In a randomized trial of 464 primary teachers in 108 English schools, those using Oak National Academy's AI lesson assistant, Aila, spent about 2.5 hours a week preparing lessons, against 3.3 hours without it. Independent reviewers found the lessons were no worse in quality.

#AIforGood

Lesson planning eats into teachers' evenings.

An independent trial for the Education Endowment Foundation found that primary teachers using Aila, an AI lesson assistant from Oak National Academy, saved about 49 minutes a week. Teachers newer to the profession, or less confident in a subject, were the most likely to gain.

#AIforGood

What could a teacher do with an extra 49 minutes a week?

That is how much time primary teachers saved on lesson preparation with Aila, Oak National Academy's AI assistant, in a randomized trial of 464 teachers. The evaluators gave the evidence a high security rating, and the lessons were no worse in quality.

#AIforGood
stories.source_name: Education Endowment Foundation evaluation report by NFER, Oct 2026
stories.og_title: Lesson planning using AI lesson assistant, Aila - A Teacher Choices Trial: Evaluation report

stories.institution: Geisinger machine-learning colorectal cancer screening outreach, with University of Hong Kong and Columbia Business School
stories.teaser: AI flags who needs a colonoscopy, and a nurse calls them
stories.headline: AI-guided colon cancer outreach at Geisinger tied to 43% lower 2-year mortality
stories.why: Real-world evaluation against matched controls, Manufacturing & Service Operations Management
stories.bullet: Two-year deaths down 43%, as AI flagged patients for colon cancer screening
texts:
Since 2019, Geisinger has used a machine learning model that reads routine blood counts, age and sex to flag patients at higher risk of colorectal cancer who are overdue for screening. Nurse coordinators then call them.

Flagged patients were 6% more likely to complete a colonoscopy within three months, and two-year mortality fell 43% relative to similar patients without outreach.

#AIforGood

Colorectal cancer is one of the most preventable causes of cancer death, if people get screened in time. Geisinger pairs an AI risk model with a phone call from a nurse who explains the test and books it.

Compared with similar patients, those reached were more likely to have a colonoscopy, and their two-year mortality was 43% lower.

#AIforGood

Who should get the call first? At Geisinger, a machine learning model answers that from blood tests already in the record, and nurses do the rest.

A study in Manufacturing & Service Operations Management found the outreach raised colonoscopy completion and cut two-year mortality by 43% relative to a comparison group.

#AIforGood
stories.og_title: AI-guided outreach increased cancer screenings and reduced mortality, new study finds
